questions.q: Why does assigning access to a group rather than an individual reduce governance risk?
options: Membership changes automatically grant or revoke access, with nothing for anyone to remember to update
Groups are technically incapable of being over-permissioned, unlike individuals
AWS and Azure both forbid assigning roles directly to individual users
Group-based access never needs to be reviewed or audited
questions.explain: When a role or policy is attached to a group, a new hire joining or someone leaving the team automatically grants or revokes their access -- no separate step to remember, unlike per-individual assignments.

questions.q: What is an access review, as described in this lesson?
options: A recurring, structured process where a resource owner periodically confirms whether each person's access is still needed
A one-time audit performed only when a security incident occurs
A feature that automatically deletes all user accounts older than one year
A synonym for a break-glass account
questions.explain: An access review is explicitly recurring, not a one-time cleanup -- it exists because access tends to persist long after it's needed unless something periodically forces a re-confirmation.

questions.q: Why is a break-glass account deliberately excluded from the group-based, least-privilege, periodically-reviewed pattern that governs everything else?
options: Because its entire purpose is to work even when normal access -- including the identity system itself -- is unavailable
Because break-glass accounts are considered low-risk and don't need any special governance
Because AWS and Azure don't support break-glass accounts, so the pattern doesn't apply to them
Because break-glass accounts are only used for testing, never in production
questions.explain: A break-glass account has to function during an identity-system outage or federation failure, so it can't depend on the same group-based/reviewed mechanisms as everything else -- instead it's vaulted, alerted on every use, and audited after every single use.

questions.q: What does just-in-time (JIT) access reduce, as distinct from the group-based and least-privilege patterns?
options: How long access exists -- rather than who has it or how broad it is
The number of people who are allowed to request access at all
The cost of running IAM services in the cloud
The need for any access reviews to ever be performed
questions.explain: Group-based assignment addresses who, least privilege addresses how broad, and JIT access addresses how long -- Entra PIM and AWS STS AssumeRole both grant time-limited, auto-expiring access rather than standing permanent access.

questions.q: What is the AWS equivalent of Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management (PIM) for shrinking the window a credential is dangerous?
options: STS AssumeRole, which issues temporary credentials with a built-in expiration
AWS Organizations, which manages the account hierarchy
AWS Config, which detects configuration drift
IAM Access Analyzer, which reviews unused permissions
questions.explain: STS AssumeRole is the mechanism this lesson identifies as AWS's parallel to Entra PIM -- both issue access that's active only for a limited window rather than standing permanently active, though IAM Access Analyzer plays the parallel role for access reviews instead.
